title: Alignment-Sensitive Minimax Rates for Spectral Algorithms with Learned Kernels
claim: Training an over-parameterized model progressively lowers the complexity profile, and the reduction grows as signal-feature misalignment increases.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid, log-log curves, colors encode training time
description: A 2x2 grid of log-log line plots. Each panel shows d†(τ) on the y-axis against τ from 1e-7 to 1e-2 on the x-axis, and each has a different misalignment level: q=1, 1.5, 2 and 3. Five colored curves in each panel mark training times t=0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 (blue, orange, green, pink, yellow). Every curve is flat at small τ and then decays. For q=1 all curves overlap, so training changes nothing. As q grows, the curves separate more and more. Later times sit well below the t=0 curve, and the gap is largest at q=3, where the profile falls by about an order of magnitude. A legend sits inside each panel. The eye goes first to the spread of curves in the q=3 panel.
caption: Evolution of span profiles during the training of an over-parameterized gradient flow. The misalignment level $q$ varies from $1$ to $3$. Fixed parameters are $n=10000$, $\sigma_0=1$, $d=5000$, $J=15$, $p=2.5$, and $\gamma=1$.
abstract: We study spectral algorithms in the setting where kernels are learned from data. We introduce the effective span dimension (ESD), an alignment-sensitive complexity measure that depends jointly on the signal, spectrum, and noise level $Ï^2$. The ESD is well-defined for arbitrary kernels and signals without requiring eigen-decay conditions or source conditions. We prove that for sequence models whose ESD is at most $K$, the minimax excess risk scales as $Ï^2 K$. Furthermore, we analyze over-parameterized gradient flow and prove that it can reduce the ESD. This finding establishes a connection between adaptive feature learning and provable improvements in generalization of spectral algorithms. We demonstrate the generality of the ESD framework by extending it to linear models and RKHS regression, and we support the theory with numerical experiments. This framework provides a novel perspective on generalization beyond traditional fixed-kernel theories.
